title: Arsenal 1 Atletico Madrid 0 (2-1 agg) – How did Arteta reach UCL final? Will it be their biggest week ever? Was Gabriel lucky?
author: James McNicholas
content:
Arsenal will play a first Champions League final in 20 years in what promises to be a grandstand finish to their season after Bukayo Saka’s goal helped the Premier League leaders eliminate Atletico Madrid.

Denied a penalty when Leandro Trossard was knocked over by Antoine Griezmann on 34 minutes, Arsenal were ahead 10 minutes later when Saka pounced on a rebound after Trossard’s shot was saved by Jan Oblak.

The two sides had drawn the first leg 1-1 in Madrid last week and the Spanish visitors were looking for a spot kick of their own when Giuliano Simeone, Atletico manager Diego’s son, rounded goalkeeper David Raya and tangled with Gabriel. They sought another soon after when Griezmann was caught by Riccardo Calafiori but referee Daniel Siebert had given an earlier foul by Atletico.

It was Arsenal who missed the next big chance, though, when the hardworking Viktor Gyokeres shot over from 12 yards after a fine Piero Hincapie cross. But with the backing of a booming atmosphere at the Emirates Stadium, Mikel Arteta’s side held out to win 2-1 on aggregate.

Paris Saint-Germain take a 5-4 lead to Germany to face Bayern Munich in Wednesday’s second semi-final decider, and the final will be played at 5pm UK time (noon ET) on Saturday, May 30, at the Puskas Arena in Budapest, Hungary.

The Athletic’s James McNicholas, Dermot Corrigan, Mark Carey and Stuart James break down the key talking points.

Could seven days at the end of May constitute the biggest week in Arsenal’s history?

If, as seems plausible, the Premier League title race runs until the season’s final day, they may have the opportunity to win it away to Crystal Palace on Sunday, May 24. Then, on the Saturday, they will be in Budapest to contest the Champions League final with Paris Saint-Germain or Bayern Munich.

It is difficult to overstate quite how enormous this could be.

Arsenal have waited 22 years for a Premier League title. They have never won a European Cup/Champions League. It is the 20th anniversary of their only final to date; a 2-1 defeat by Barcelona in Paris. The European Cup/Champions League remains the sole major omission on their roll call of honours.

This season is headed towards a nerve-shredding, mouth-watering, potentially trophy-clutching finale.

The team endured a wobble in March and April that saw speculative talk of a quadruple dissipate. Any anguish will be long forgotten if Arteta can land this extraordinary double.

James McNicholas

Just like last week’s first leg, much of the controversy throughout the game focused on penalty claims and counter-claims.

Arsenal felt they might have had one midway through the first half, when Griezmann made a clumsy challenge on Trossard near the 18-yard line, which the officials deemed not sufficient to blow for a foul.

At the start of the second half, it was Atletico’s turn — when Giuliano Simeone quickly pounced on William Saliba’s error, and got to the ball before goalkeeper David Raya.

But the Atletico man’s touch was a little heavy, and Gabriel got back to put on enough pressure so that he was unable to get a shot off.

Replays showed that Gabriel had wrapped an arm around Simeone, which was enough to prevent the Argentinian producing a clean attempt at goal.

The visitors claimed vigorously for a penalty, but the officials quickly decided that no action should be taken, to the relief of both Arsenal centre-backs.

Moments later came another Atletico claim, as Griezmann had space in the box to drive in a shot which Raya palmed out. Marc Pubill went for the rebound with Gabriel, which they both missed, and it fell to Griezmann, who was then taken out by Calafiori.

Again, Atletico were loud with their claims, and Arsenal’s Italian defender did seem to have made a clear foul, but the officials appeared to believe the action by Pubill earlier made what happened afterwards irrelevant.

“Sometimes the VAR gives, sometimes it takes away,” said Diego Simeone after the first leg.

It happened again tonight.

Dermot Corrigan

Arsenal can expect to be the outsiders in the Champions League final against Paris Saint-Germain or Bayern Munich, but their style of football could be the perfect antidote to the way whichever of those sides triumph in Munich tomorrow like to play the game.

To borrow a line often used in boxing, styles make fights. You do not have to be the biggest or the best, but you do have to nullify the strengths of the opposition you face.

Arsenal might not be as free-flowing in attack as the French and German giants, but their defensive solidity is more likely to frustrate them in Budapest than was the case in that nine-goal semi-final first leg in Paris — with a discipline that would rarely see the game open up in a way that would play into the hands of Arteta’s counterpart, whether that is PSG’s Luis Enrique or Vincent Kompany of Bayern.

It would also be oversimplistic to suggest that Arsenal’s biggest chance of victory on the night would be to play in a reactive manner to their opponents. They are still unbeaten in this season’s Champions League, unlike PSG and Bayern, and some of their best performances in Europe have come when teams go toe-to-toe with them.

Add in their widely-known set piece threat, individual quality and unwavering physicality and Arsenal should be confident that they can leave Hungary with the first European Cup in club history.

Finishing top of the table in the eight-match league phase afforded Arsenal the luxury of home second legs throughout the knockout rounds. On this auspicious occasion, the supporters made sure to take full advantage of it.

Home fans congregated on the nearby Hornsey Road roundabout to greet both teams’ coaches as they arrived. The Atletico bus received a hostile welcome, before red flares were lit to signal the arrival of the Arsenal one. These were unprecedented scenes at the Emirates itself: north London passion with a continental tint.

The club and their supporters have taken inspiration from some of Europe’s best atmospheres.

Before kick-off, they unveiled their largest tifo to date: a huge banner suspended from the roof of the East Stand. It had a nautical theme — a ship setting sail above the words “Over Land and Sea” (Leicester not pictured).

Arsenal’s fans carried the atmosphere through the rendition of The Angel and into the game. Atletico, to their credit, did not appear phased by it. Simeone’s players are veterans of heated Madrid derbies, after all.

When Saka scored what proved the only goal, he ran straight to the corner of the pitch to embrace the home support.

That celebration is one of several images from tonight’s game that will be immortalised as a cherished piece of Arsenal iconography.

James McNicholas

Myles Lewis-Skelly in central midfield in the second leg of a Champions League semi-final? It was a huge and bold call on Mikel Arteta’s part, bearing in mind the 19-year-old had never started a game in that position for Arsenal’s first team until the league win against Fulham on Saturday.

The expectation was that Martin Zubimendi would return after being rested for that match. But in a season when Lewis-Skelly has been marginalised and eased out of the left-back spot by a combination of Calafiori and Hincapie, it was the teenager’s name in the starting XI alongside Declan Rice.

The position is not entirely unfamiliar territory for Lewis-Skelly — he played in centre midfield throughout his academy years and excelled — but this was a night with a Champions League final place on the line against a vastly experienced Atletico side.

How would he cope? The answer is with remarkable maturity.

Neat and tidy on the ball, Lewis-Skelly dovetailed superbly with Rice. He was caught in possession by Marcos Llorente in the first 10 minutes when he tried to use his body to protect the ball and turn – something that he loves to do – and the Spaniard read his intentions. But that moment didn’t faze him.

Moments later, Lewis-Skelly was receiving deep inside Arsenal territory again and rapping an excellent pass between the lines and into the feet of Calafiori — a moment that was typical of his desire to play forward and his bravery on the ball. He also used his strength to excellent effect to hold off Julian Alvarez close to the byline before rolling an inviting ball across the six-yard box.

It was, all in all, a hugely impressive performance from a player whose season has turned around spectacularly in the space of four days.

When he departed in the 73rd minute, to be replaced by Zubimendi, it was to a standing ovation and with his chant – “49, 49 (his shirt number), Lewis-Skelly” – reverberating around the stadium.

Stuart James

It would be difficult for Arsenal fans to hold Saka in higher esteem than they already do, but his recent absence due to an Achilles injury has made them appreciate his qualities even more.

After a goal and an assist in the first half of Saturday’s Premier League clash with Fulham, Saka opened (and closed) the scoring against Atletico tonight with a poacher’s finish.

For all that Noni Madueke offers energy and a drop of a shoulder, the end-product that Saka has shown is where he stands out on Arsenal’s right flank.

Able to go on the inside or outside of the defender facing him, Saka’s delivery is exceptional more often than not — with an ability to impact the game in some way. His finish here made it 14 goal involvements (nine goals, five assists) for him in his 14 Champions League games at the Emirates.

It is not just Saka’s individual quality, but what his threat can offer towards the wider team dynamic.

Before his substitution approaching the hour mark, the 24-year-old was drifting inside into central areas, which allowed Ben White to stay by the touchline to offer Arsenal’s width. When Saka did the latter, White made underlapping runs ahead of the ball to stretch Atletico’s shape and give his fellow England international the option of a pass or a run inside.

Having a fresh Saka returning to the team has come at the perfect time.

With the next few weeks being the most important Arsenal have had for decades, Arteta will be desperate to keep him fit for the final chapter of their season.

It was a very attacking XI from manager Simeone — with all of Griezmann, son Guiliano, Ademola Lookman and Alvarez in the team, which suggested they were going to look to take the game to Arsenal.

But Atletico spent much of the first half defending deep near their penalty area, with a lack of ball players in midfield meaning they found it very difficult to get enough possession to get a grip on the match. Simeone was urging his defenders to move higher, but Arsenal kept being able to push them back.

And this Atletico squad are not good at defending deep — the goal just before half-time was a systems breakdown from their point of view. David Hancko was at fault in allowing Gyokeres in behind the defence in the first place, then Oblak was not sure whether to come or stay on his line. When the cross came in, Pubill headed it straight to Trossard. Oblak did well to get a hand to the shot, but Robin Le Normand and Matteo Ruggeri combined so that Saka was both unmarked and onside when the ball fell to him.

Simeone’s eagerness to make changes after the break showed how his initial plan had not worked. Soon after the hour, he had already made all five substitutions — and four of his starting attackers were off the pitch (although Lookman and Alvarez were not 100 per cent fit).

The closing stages were full of frenzy and effort from the visitors, but Raya was not really troubled in the Arsenal goal.

Atletico ended up caught between two stools. They no longer have the tough defenders to dig in, like Simeone’s 2014 or 2016 teams, who did make Champions League finals, but they also lacked the spark and quality in attack to really cause Arsenal enough problems.

Dermot Corrigan

Speaking to Amazon Prime, the game’s UK broadcaster, Arteta said: “It’s an amazing night to live this kind of moment with the players and everyone at the club. An incredible feeling. It makes sense with all of the things we do and we go through, and I see so many happy faces and proud of what we’re doing.

“It was unbelievable right from the beginning — the supporters waiting for us outside the stadium, the energy and passion that they put in, so it was just great to win this. They (the fans) set the standards and we’ve tried to catch up with them. We struggled so many years to give that joy back and the pride in their eyes was beautiful to watch.”

Asked what impressed him most about Arsenal’s performance, Arteta answered: “The togetherness. It was very difficult to make certain decisions, and I feel a lot for the boys. I know generally how good people they are, and some of them, I talked to them this afternoon and apologised and said, ‘I’m going to play the same team’ (as against Fulham on Saturday) and the reaction immediately was, ‘Boss, I’m here when you need me’, and they gave me a hug.”

And on it being Saka who got the winning goal: “It had to be someone very special, and certainly he is very special with me and the boys and everyone attached with this club. If it had to be someone scoring that goal, it probably had to be him.”

Diego Simeone said Atletico’s players and fans should be applauded for a “very good” season in the Champions League as the team “gave everything, went further than expected.”

“It’s a pity as we deserved, over the two legs, to at least reach extra-time and battle for more,” he told Movistar TV.

“The first leg we had chances to score more goals, which we did not take. Today, we were better after the break, played in their half, made chances. But all the small details did not go our way.”

On the penalty appeals, he added: “There’s nothing to say, we’re out of the competition, we congratulate Arsenal who have a team and a coach that I like, with a coherent line of work, and financial power which allows them to compete in this way.”
